# Research Memorandum: Independent Criticism and Alternative Explanations

## Scope and Method

This memorandum covers file pages 118 through 235 of *How the Mind Works*, comprising the end of Chapter 3 "Revenge of the Nerds," all of Chapter 4 "The Mind's Eye," all of Chapter 5 "Good Ideas," and the first portion of Chapter 6 "Hotheads." My assigned job is to attack the provisional theory using what the source actually says, to identify alternative mechanisms the source leaves open, and to propose discriminating tests. I keep Steven Pinker's claims distinct from our engineering proposals throughout. I flag extraction gaps where they affect the argument.

## The Strongest Challenge: Grounded Records Are Not Enough Without Built-In Assumptions

The provisional theory proposes "grounded structured records of observations, events and possible actions" over "calibrated sensor records." This section of the source delivers the most damaging evidence yet against any hope that calibration is a neutral preprocessing step. Pinker's discussion of inverse optics (file pages 126 through 127) states that the deduction of an object's shape and substance from its projection is an ill-posed problem with no unique solution. An elliptical retinal image could come from an oval seen head-on or a circle seen at a slant; a gray patch could come from snow in shade or coal in sunlight (file page 127). Vision converts these unsolvable problems into solvable ones by adding premises about how the world is on average put together (file page 127).

This is not a minor engineering detail. It means that "calibrated sensor records" cannot be produced by any passive transduction mechanism. Every stage of perception requires assumptions that are not derivable from the input. The shape analyzer assumes the current viewpoint is generic rather than deliberately aligned (file pages 143 through 144). The lightness analyzer assumes uniform illumination and an average scene (file pages 145 through 146). The shading analyzer assumes uniform surface lightness and matte materials (file pages 148 through 149). The stereo matcher assumes each mark is anchored to one surface, that one mark matches at most one other mark, and that matter is cohesive and smooth (file pages 138 through 139).

The provisional theory says "initial structure and goal priorities are supplied explicitly," but it does not say what perceptual assumptions are supplied. If the machine is given none, it cannot construct grounded records at all. If it is given many, the theory has smuggled in a large innate endowment under the label "calibration." A discriminating test: present the machine with the Ames room (file pages 128 through 129) or Adelson's zigzag drawings (file pages 142 through 143). If the machine's records are faithful to the retinal projection, it will not see the illusion; if they are faithful to the world, they must embody assumptions that produce the illusion when violated. Either behavior tells us what assumptions are built in.

## The Adelson and Pentland Alternative: Cost Minimization Across Competing Experts

The source offers a concrete alternative to the provisional theory's "bounded deterministic program construction." Adelson and Pentland's workshop parable (file pages 147 through 155) proposes that shape, lighting, and reflectance specialists each propose interpretations, and a supervisory scheme coordinates them by minimizing a cost in which improbable guesses are expensive (file pages 152 through 153). Their computer program implements this: the shape specialist seeks the most regular, planar, compact three-dimensional form; the lighting specialist positions a single distant light; the reflectance specialist paints whatever discrepancy remains (file pages 153 through 154).

This is a genuine alternative mechanism. Instead of constructing programs that predict observations, the machine could maintain multiple competing interpretations of the same input and settle on the cheapest one. The provisional theory's "seek observations on which candidates disagree" is an active-learning strategy; Adelson and Pentland's is a passive disambiguation strategy. They are not incompatible, but they solve different problems. The provisional theory must say which it uses for perception and which for higher cognition.

A discriminating test: give the machine an ambiguous image like the fanfold that flips in depth (file page 154). The Adelson and Pentland program assigns equal costs to both interpretations and picks one at random; the source notes that if the specialists passed guesses in a constraint network, the program might flip between them as people do (file page 154). If the provisional theory's machine constructs one model and commits to it, it will not exhibit bistable perception. If it maintains competing candidates, we can measure whether its flips follow the constraint-satisfaction dynamics described at file pages 138 through 139.

## The Constraint-Satisfaction Alternative to Program Construction

Pinker presents Marr and Poggio's constraint network for stereo vision (file pages 138 through 139) as a mechanism in which thousands of processors make tentative guesses and negotiate until a global solution emerges. Units for matches along the same line of sight inhibit one another; units for neighboring points at nearby depths excite one another (file page 139). This is a parallel, distributed, iterative mechanism, not a sequential program search.

The provisional theory proposes "bounded deterministic program construction," which sounds like sequential search through a space of programs. The source leaves open whether constraint satisfaction is a better mechanism for the perceptual grounding problem. Constraint satisfaction handles the chicken-and-egg problem of stereo matching (file page 138) without enumerating hypotheses. Program construction would have to enumerate candidate matchings, which the source shows to be combinatorially explosive: with a hundred marks there are almost ten thousand possible matches (file page 134).

A discriminating test: present the machine with a random-dot stereogram (file pages 129 through 130) containing many marks. Measure whether the machine's processing time grows with the number of possible matches, as enumeration predicts, or remains roughly constant per mark, as parallel constraint satisfaction predicts. Also measure whether the solution emerges gradually, with partial contours appearing before the whole, as the source describes for human perception (file page 139).

## The Reference Frame Problem: A Hidden Prerequisite for Grounded Records

The provisional theory says nothing about reference frames. The source shows this is a critical omission. The two-and-a-half-dimensional sketch that vision delivers is specified in retinal coordinates, which are useless as soon as the eyes move (file pages 155 through 156). To use visual information, the machine needs reference frames that stay put as the eyes, head, and body move. Pinker describes several: a head-centered frame shifted by copies of eye-movement commands (file page 155), body-centered and world-centered frames possibly driven by copies of neck and body commands (file page 155), a gravity-aligned frame from the vestibular system (file pages 155 through 156), and object-centered frames aligned on axes of elongation and symmetry (file pages 158 through 159).

Each of these is a piece of machinery the provisional theory must specify. If "grounded structured records" are stored in retinal coordinates, they will not support recognition across viewpoints or action planning. If they are stored in object-centered coordinates, the machine needs a mechanism for aligning frames on objects, which is itself a nontrivial perceptual achievement. The source shows that people use multiple strategies for shape recognition: object-centered geon models for some shapes, multiple stored views for others, and mental rotation for unfamiliar orientations (file pages 164 through 165). The provisional theory must say which it implements and how.

A discriminating test: train the machine on a shape at one orientation, then present it at a new orientation. If recognition time increases with angular distance, the machine is using mental rotation. If it is constant, the machine is using an object-centered frame. If it is fast only at trained orientations, the machine is using multiple views. The source shows that people use all three (file pages 164 through 165), so a single-strategy machine would be a poor model of human shape recognition.

## The Compositionality Problem Reappears in Geons

The previous memorandum raised compositionality as a challenge. This section reinforces it. Biederman's geon theory (file pages 159 through 160) proposes that objects are described as combinations of simple geometric parts joined by attachment relations like "above," "beside," and "end to end." This is explicitly combinatorial: a small number of geons and attachments combine into an astronomical number of objects (file page 160).

But the source also shows that geons are not sufficient. Many natural objects have complicated fractal shapes that geons reduce to crude approximations (file page 160). Particular faces cannot be built from geons without confusing one person with another (file page 160). And the pure geon theory is contaminated by multiple views and mental rotation (file pages 164 through 165). The provisional theory's "elementary operations and previously constructed subprograms" must specify what plays the role of geons and attachments. If the elementary operations are arbitrary, the composition problem is unsolved. If they are geometric primitives, the theory has adopted a specific hypothesis about shape representation that the source shows to be incomplete.

A discriminating test: present the machine with a fractal shape like a tree or mountain and a geon-composable shape like a cup. If the machine represents both in the same format, inspect how it handles the fractal. If it uses different formats, the theory needs multiple representation systems, which raises the question of how they interact.

## Temporal Memory: The Source Offers No Episode Mechanism

The provisional theory distinguishes "episode-specific records from reusable knowledge." This section of the source provides almost no support for how episode records are constructed or maintained. The discussion of mental imagery (file pages 167 through 174) shows that images are fragmentary, that people recall glimpses of parts and arrange them in a mental tableau (file page 174), and that memory images must be labeled and organized within a propositional superstructure (file pages 174 through 175). The penny experiment (file page 173) shows that visual memories are not accurate pictures of whole objects: the median subject remembered three of eight features, half in the wrong place.

This is a serious obstacle for the provisional theory. If episode records are pictorial, they are fragmentary and unreliable. If they are propositional, they need a labeling and retrieval system that the source does not describe. The source also shows that people cannot reconstruct an image of an entire visual scene (file page 174), which means that any theory of temporal memory based on storing complete snapshots is wrong.

A discriminating test: have the machine observe a scene, then query it about details after a delay. Compare its accuracy for central versus peripheral details, for whole objects versus parts, and for spatial relations versus object identities. If its performance matches the penny experiment, its memory is imagistic and fragmentary. If it is uniformly accurate, it is using a different mechanism, possibly propositional, which the source does not describe.

## Goals and Emotions: The Source Shows Goals Are Not Simple Priorities

The provisional theory says "initial structure and goal priorities are supplied explicitly." The previous memorandum raised the Samaritan robot problem. This section deepens the challenge. Pinker's discussion of emotions (file pages 217 through 219) argues that emotions are mechanisms that set the brain's highest-level goals. Once triggered, an emotion triggers a cascade of subgoals and sub-subgoals (file page 218). Fear is triggered by signals of impending harm and lights up short-term goals of fleeing or deflecting danger, plus longer-term goals of avoiding the hazard in future (file page 218).

This is not a fixed priority list. Goals are dynamically selected by emotional states, which are themselves triggered by context. The provisional theory's "explicit goal priorities" would behave like Samaritan I in novel situations. The source also shows that emotions are not irrational impulses but well-engineered software modules that work in harmony with the intellect (file page 217). A machine without something like emotions would have no way of knowing what to do next (file pages 217 through 218).

A discriminating test: place the machine in a situation where multiple goals are relevant and vary the context. If the machine's goal selection is fixed, it will not adapt. If it is context-sensitive, inspect how the triggering works. The source suggests that emotions are triggered by "propitious moments" (file page 218) but does not specify the trigger mechanism.

## The Frame Problem Reappears in Logic

The previous memorandum raised the frame problem through Dennett's robot parable. This section raises it again in the context of logic. Pinker notes that any true statement can spawn an infinite number of true but useless new ones (file page 195). Unless the inferencer has all the time in the world, it must guess which implications to explore (file page 195). The guessing cannot come from logic; it comes from assuming a cooperative conversational partner (file page 195).

The provisional theory's "seek observations on which candidates disagree" could become exhaustive enumeration of implications. The source offers no solution but suggests that content-specific inference rules, like Cosmides' cheater-detector (file pages 196 through 197), constrain the search. The provisional theory must specify what constrains its search.

## Consciousness: A Boundary the Theory Must Respect

Pinker's discussion of mental imagery (file pages 167 through 174) shows that images share brain areas with perception but are somehow different (file page 169). The source does not claim that implementing imagery produces sentience. The provisional theory does not claim consciousness, and this is correct. But it must not imply that its mechanisms are sufficient for sentience. The source is clear that the computational theory of mind offers no clear answer to the problem of sentience (from the previous section, file page 82).

## Alternative Mechanisms the Source Leaves Open

The source leaves open several alternatives to the provisional theory's bounded deterministic program construction. First, constraint satisfaction networks (file pages 138 through 139) for perceptual disambiguation. Second, cost minimization across competing experts (file pages 147 through 155) for scene interpretation. Third, multiple stored views with mental rotation (file pages 164 through 165) for shape recognition. Fourth, pictorial arrays with graphic operations like zooming, panning, and scanning (file pages 170 through 171) for spatial reasoning. Fifth, propositional superstructures organizing fragmentary images (file pages 174 through 175) for memory. The provisional theory must say which of these it uses and why.

## Unresolved Questions for the Next Section

The next section should address: how perceptual assumptions are specified and implemented; how reference frames are constructed and maintained; how episode records are stored and retrieved; how emotional states trigger and prioritize goals; how search is constrained without exhaustive enumeration; whether constraint satisfaction or program construction is the better mechanism for grounding; and how multiple representation formats interact. The source also raises the question of how the machine distinguishes its own mental images from perceptions, which the source suggests is important for avoiding hallucinations and false memories (file page 169). Finally, the source's discussion of metaphor (file pages 205 through 210) suggests that abstract thought may be built by co-opting concrete representations, which is a possible mechanism for the provisional theory's "previously constructed subprograms" but one that the source does not fully specify.
